params.question: A single episode of painless visible haematuria in an otherwise well patient requires no further investigation if the urine subsequently clears.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: This statement is false. The video's 66-year-old smoker had just one painless bleed and felt entirely well, yet he has the classic presentation of bladder cancer. Malignant causes bleed intermittently, and wellness does not exclude cancer. Never be falsely reassured by a single normal result.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct. Painless visible haematuria is urological malignancy until proven otherwise. Bladder cancer bleeds intermittently, so a single episode that clears spontaneously is the textbook presentation — not a reason for reassurance. A complete work-up with CT urogram and cystoscopy is mandatory.

interactions.label: On urine microscopy, a patient's sample shows dysmorphic red blood cells and red

params.question: On urine microscopy, a patient's sample shows dysmorphic red blood cells and red-cell casts. This combination indicates bleeding from which source?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Bladder wall bleeding is a surgical (urological) source that produces isomorphic (normal-shaped) red cells and may produce clots, but not red-cell casts.

Correct. Red cells become dysmorphic by squeezing through the glomerular filtration barrier, and casts form within the renal tubules. Together these are pathognomonic of glomerular (medical) bleeding, warranting nephrology referral rather than surgery.
The renal pelvis is lined by urothelium — bleeding here is a surgical source and produces isomorphic red cells without red-cell casts.
Prostatic bleeding is a urological source that produces isomorphic red cells. Red-cell casts only form within renal tubules downstream of a damaged glomerulus.

overallFeedback.feedback: Dysmorphic red cells are distorted by passage through the glomerular barrier, and casts form in the tubules. These findings point to a medical (glomerular) cause, not a surgical one.
Well done. Dysmorphic red cells and red-cell casts together are the hallmark of glomerular disease — always redirect such patients to nephrology.

interactions.label: A 62-year-old man had one episode of painless visible haematuria two weeks ago.

params.question: A 62-year-old man had one episode of painless visible haematuria two weeks ago. His urine dipstick today is negative. What is the most appropriate next step?

answers.text: Reassure the patient and advise follow-up only if bleeding recurs

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Reassurance without investigation is dangerous. A single painless bleed may be the only warning of an early, curable malignancy. Bladder cancer bleeds intermittently.

answers.text: Prescribe antibiotics and repeat the dipstick in one month

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Antibiotics treat infection, not malignancy. A negative dipstick today does not exclude a tumour that bled intermittently two weeks ago.

answers.text: Proceed with CT urogram and flexible cystoscopy

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Painless visible haematuria demands a complete work-up regardless of current dipstick findings. CT urogram images the upper tract; flexible cystoscopy visualises the bladder directly. Both are mandatory because each detects lesions the other misses.

answers.text: Request urine cytology alone and discharge if negative

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Negative urine cytology does not exclude malignancy — its sensitivity is limited, especially for low-grade tumours. Both CT urogram and cystoscopy are still required.

overallFeedback.feedback: Remember: bladder cancer bleeds intermittently. A negative dipstick today does not close the case. The complete work-up — CT urogram for the upper tract and flexible cystoscopy for the bladder — is mandatory.

Exactly right. The non-negotiable rule: unexplained painless visible haematuria demands CT urogram plus cystoscopy before any reassurance — a snapshot urinalysis can be clear even when cancer is present.

interactions.label: In bladder cancer, the single most important factor that determines whether the

params.question: In bladder cancer, the single most important factor that determines whether the bladder can be preserved is:

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Grade influences prognosis and adjuvant therapy choices but does not independently determine whether the bladder can be saved. A high-grade non-muscle-invasive tumour is still managed with TURBT and intravesical therapy.

answers.text: Whether the tumour has invaded the detrusor muscle

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Non-muscle-invasive tumours (Ta, T1, CIS) can be managed with transurethral resection and intravesical therapy, preserving the bladder. Once the tumour invades the detrusor (T2 or above), radical cystectomy with urinary diversion is typically required.

answers.text: The presence or absence of haematuria at diagnosis

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Haematuria is a presenting symptom, not a staging criterion. Its presence or absence does not determine the depth of invasion or the choice between bladder preservation and cystectomy.

answers.text: The size of the tumour on cystoscopy

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Tumour size is clinically relevant but secondary to depth of invasion. A small tumour invading the detrusor is more consequential for management than a large superficial one.

overallFeedback.feedback: The critical question is depth of invasion into the detrusor muscle. TURBT provides the histology and invasion depth. Non-muscle-invasive disease (Ta/T1/CIS) preserves the bladder; muscle-invasive disease (T2+) typically requires radical cystectomy.
Spot on. The muscle-invasion divide — answered by TURBT biopsy — is the central decision point: preserve the bladder or remove it.

params.question: A contrast-enhanced CT scan reveals a 3.5 cm renal mass confined to the kidney with no evidence of renal vein thrombus or metastases. What is the most appropriate surgical management?

answers.text: Radical nephrectomy with removal of Gerota's fascia

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Radical nephrectomy is reserved for larger or locally advanced tumours. For a small tumour confined to the kidney, removing the entire kidney sacrifices renal function unnecessarily.

Correct. A 3.5 cm mass is T1a (≤4 cm, confined to the kidney). Partial nephrectomy preserves renal parenchyma and long-term renal function while achieving equivalent oncological outcomes for small, localised tumours.
Transurethral resection is used for bladder tumours accessed via the urethra. Renal masses require open or laparoscopic surgical excision — they cannot be reached endoscopically.

answers.text: Tyrosine kinase inhibitor therapy as first-line treatment

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Tyrosine kinase inhibitors and immunotherapy are reserved for metastatic renal cell carcinoma. In localised disease without metastases, surgery is the curative treatment.

overallFeedback.feedback: This 3.5 cm mass, confined with no thrombus or metastases, is stage T1a. The preferred approach is partial nephrectomy — preserving healthy kidney tissue. Radical nephrectomy is reserved for larger or advanced tumours; RCC resists chemotherapy and radiotherapy, so surgery is the curative tool.
Well done. For T1a RCC (≤4 cm, confined), nephron-sparing surgery preserves kidney tissue and protects long-term renal function — staging drives the surgical decision.
